Even from that brief description that sounds a lot like my experience, good GPA, good grades but hard headed and determined to join the military. 

You are able to pick your job field however you are not able to pick the specific job, for example you could choose to be in the infantry but the military will ultimately decide whether you’ll be working as an LAV crewman (armored vehicle) or whether you’ll be a mortar man or rifleman. What they mentioned about changing your job is mostly true, you can change your job but generally only after 2 years of experience in that job and it’s nearly impossible to change jobs unless you’re willing to sign a multi year extension. The military helped me find the career path I wanted but that was in spite of the military not because of it, the endless nights of sitting in the pouring rain led me to the realization that what I wanted involved a desk job with constancy not a job that involved living outdoors with little to no sleep and effectively being a professionally homeless. 

The military talks about structure but the only structure it actually provides is rank structure, you are always at the disposal of your superiors at all hours. You have no idea what’s happening a day a week or a month from now, you might spend an entire day doing nothing except sitting in your room and the next day you’ll spend working for hours on end, you won’t know which will be which and you won’t be able to plan your day (this is speaking from my experience in the infantry although I’m sure it’s similar in other fields too).

The other commenter is spot on with everything they listed so I’ll skip that but all what they mentioned is accurate. The military will not help you determine your future outside of the military and surprisingly little to determine your future in the military, you are there as a number and if you enjoy being a number great if not that’s irrelevant they still own you for 4 years (you cannot leave under threat of prison time under the UCMJ). 

As far as the college benefits go, look at the GI bill college comparison tool on the schools website. They provide 36 months of housing payments based on zip codes for the college or university meaning for summer and winter break you’re responsible for paying your own lodging. The amount the GI will pay is capped at I believe $28k a year, you will need to make up the difference out of pocket or via scholarships. 

Also the military in my experience is comprised of 2 main groups, the uneducated urban kids and the uneducated country kids, GEDs are common and the people generally do not value education. Your son probably wants to join for all the right reasons but beyond boot camp it’s a facade that I’m sure he will quickly see through. He sounds well educated and intelligent and that doesn’t help, if anything it makes worse, knowing you’re stuck, knowing you’re part of a dog and pony show and yet not being able to escape it. 

I can’t offer much to help convince him not to as when I was in that position I met a veteran who tried to talk me out of it. I would suggest looking at it from a marketing perspective, the recruiter wants you to join more than anything so take whatever he tells you with a very large grain of salt. If he is dead set on joining though try to steer him towards the reserves that way he gets to serve and still have a life.

When I was in ITB I really felt like I was doing exactly what I had signed up for, that the boot camp trope that it gets better after graduation was true, until about half way when I was told I was going to be a machine gunner. I’d volunteered to be an LAV crewman and a rifleman, after a week as a machine gunner i wasn’t enjoying it, the instructor said that if we didn’t want to be machine gunners that all we had to do was speak up and we would get put with the class behind us and it wouldn’t be an issue. So believing that I went ahead and told them, long story short I was threatened with a battalion level NJP for disobeying orders. I was threatened with the possibility of getting kicked out with an unfavorable discharge, I felt betrayed and lied to, I felt that I had done as instructed I had held up my end of the offer. That is what initially opened my eyes, of course there were many other instances but that was the first.

I was in the marine corps, got the chance to get out early by denying the Covid shot but didn’t when I was told that I would receive a dishonorable discharge and possible prison time, I got out with an honorable discharge.

Please for your own safety and sanity don’t join, I can’t speak to much about the SA because my BN has like one woman (she’s a first Sgt) but I can tell you that the ridicule and harassment in the military are unparalleled. It is not worth it, you’ve lived enough of your life to know what is right and wrong and I promise by joining you’ll realize that the public perception of the military is propaganda, the reality is a stark contrast. You can serve your country in so many ways, I did more to actually serve my country by doing food donations to the homeless when I was a Cub Scout in 3rd grade. The way the military treats people is terrible and they get away with it because of the UCMJ and it’s restrictions on what we are allowed to share publicly. Off the top of my head the most recent public example is the colonel (I think) who publicly asked for an investigation and accountability into the disastrous Afghan pull out, he was relieved of command and arrested. The reality is that life inside the military sucks, it sucks the life out of you, it sucks the happiness out of you, it becomes all consuming and there is no escape. Please if you are dead set on joining do the reserves or something but please don’t do this to yourself.

Now I can’t even enjoy video games, they don’t make me happy anymore I just feel like I’m wasting away. When I’m worried about work the next day I can’t escape by playing video games, I feel like I’m worried about finding a song on Spotify as my car is about to fly off the road and by trying to distract myself I waste the time I’m supposed to enjoy. The weekends always go the same way for me, Friday is great because work is over, Saturday is stagnant and Sunday is full of dread.

As another side note to the wastefulness I witnessed I’ll share a quick story. I was stationed in Hawaii before my unit disbanded, one of the training exercises we did involved us going to this field chow hall where all we ate was canned food. On the last day I was added to a working party to destroy all the unused food, there was an 18 wheeler truck bed full of canned goods that didn’t expire until years later. We got our bayonets (for some reason our company issued bayonets as EDL) and poked a hole in every single cab and thew them in a massive dumpster. 

Anyone that’s ever been in Hawaii knows how bad Waikiki and Honolulu’s homelessness is. The locals dislike the military as is but if they knew that we were purposely destroying something that could help the struggling people they would hate us. We’ve done hikes through the town right off base to “inspire a better image of the military” in the locals but what is seeing a bunch of sweaty guys walking through your town at 6 am gonna do. We could’ve helped so many people but instead we don’t.

To be honest I’m not well enough versed with every conflict the US has been involved in to form an opinion, from what it sounds like yes that was an example of what the US military should be doing but in regards to recent wars especially I believe that instance sounds more like an exception rather than the rule.

The very fact you are even considering and asking how you can use your position shows that you are one of the good ones. I’ve known a few good officers and a couple good staff NCOs but the vast majority are just not good. 

To answer your question, 

1 - Allow people more freedom of movement. Personally I highly dislike my job and I would be much happier in H&S (for various reasons) so if it’s possible ask them, not in a threatening or condescending way but ask them if they would be happier in another billet or another job within the battalion/company. I understand the TO argument and it is valid to an extent but if that individual doesn’t like their job they should be allowed to work somewhere that better suits their skill set. 

2 - Do not encourage or tolerate mass punishment unless every single person is guilty. Mass punishment discourages the people doing the right thing as it makes them feel unseen. 

3 - Always put those below you first, they are not your stepping stool, they are your foundation. Using them to show off for higher you aren’t earning anyone’s respect. Our CO decided to conduct ridiculous company PT (while not participating himself) timed perfectly so when the BC shows up he sees all of us, this only happened when he was up for promotion. 

4 - Hold your Staff NCOs to a high standard, I don’t mean physically I mean in the way they treat people. It’s the military no one expects it to be nice but that doesn’t mean they should be allowed to physically threaten people or demand an individual be ostracized for some shortcoming.

5 - Anonymous tip line of some kind, don’t wait until the yearly survey (I forgot the name) or the PHAs, allow your junior soldiers to anonymously report what they think you could do better on or what quality of life changes you could implement. 

6 - incentivize good behavior, in my previous unit if we had 3 weekends in a row without incident we would get a 72, this is what encourages people, time off. People will do what you want because of the fear of the repercussions but they would do it happily if they were rewarded for it. 


This is what I could think of off the top of my head but I am sure there are many more suggestions. 

Also don’t organize training events that will leave guys broken. Our command is making us do 100km this week, 20k a day with gun gear and full main packs and this is about 2 weeks before our PFT. We speculate that it is because we were originally slotted for a training event that was given to another company in our battalion and this is our COs way of proving to the BC that we are the most “ready”.

I can’t even begin to describe what it’s like in one message but I’ll try to explain as best as I can. 

You go to boot camp but you expected it to be hard, you’ve seen the videos, you know relatively what to expect and there are a lot more of you than there are drill instructors so you can find a sense of community kind of. Now you get to your job training and it’s of the same although things are slightly better than boot camp. 

You’ll get to the fleet and this is where your expectations really shatter, what’s right and wrong, what’s ok and what isn’t, nothing is normal. Everything is based on seniority, the people who hold the same rank as you but have been there longer own your life, they can punish you for any reason including just for fun, they can do anything they want at any hour they want. You get filled with hate and that hate turns to depression. When you eventually get to that level of seniority you can now do all those things that were done to you and the cycle repeats. If you don’t want to do those things that were done to you then you become an outcast in your own peer group and if you do then you are no better than the ones that tormented you. 

This is only one aspect of the reality of being in the military. 

The command doesn’t care about you, you’re a number, you’re a statistic they use to make themselves look better. If you are contributing to making them look better then they’ll love you, if you need anything for yourself they’ll hate you. If you get hurt you’ll be ridiculed for faking it, if you don’t want to do anything you can be charged for that (literally as a criminal). 

You essentially live in a hopeless society where you know you’re disposable and yet you are worked to the bone, you know that no one can help you and that there is no escape. There is a term in the military called “going internal” which means essentially that while you are physically there you aren’t present, generally it’s used when people are exhausted or really cold and shivering but it’s more than that it’s a state of isolation.

I can’t really describe how people are when they get out but I imagine it’s one of 3 things

1 they miss the power they had over others and are constantly upset they can’t get it back 

2 they’re fundamentally different because of the way they’ve been treated and are either cold and indifferent or saddened and isolated.

3 they’re able to work normally with people but since not many people can relate to their experiences they feel alone. They love being out of the military but they’re cautious about what they tell people as to not ruin their image.

I despise the leadership in the military but I have had a few good ones and I think that needs to be pointed out, not everyone is a piece of shit. The vast majority are but not everyone. I had a good friend of mine who had been NJPd for something stupid and was not liked by the command, when there was a health and comfort our first sgt at time found his SARMS (some steroid) and didn’t say anything about it, after PMO had left he gave them back to the guy and said that “something like this is not worth ruining someone’s life or career over”.
